title: NHIA Renewal: Protecting Accreditation with Incomplete Data
brief: A hospital in Kano, Nigeria is renewing its accreditation with the Nigeria Health Insurance Authority (NHIA). NHIA requires quarterly submission of five indicators: bed occupancy rate, average length of stay, nosocomial infection rate, maternal mortality ratio, and under-5 mortality rate. The hospital's health management information system (HMIS) has complete data for three of the five indicators, but the nosocomial infection rate and under-5 mortality rate have not been routinely collected.

task.stem: Which action best protects the hospital's accreditation eligibility during the renewal process?

options.label: Submit data for the three available indicators, include a written explanation for the two missing indicators, and attach a corrective action plan with a clear timeline for establishing routine data collection.
Calculate estimated values for the two missing indicators based on national averages and submit them alongside the three complete indicators.
Request an extension from NHIA without submitting any data, so there is more time to collect the missing indicators.
Submit only the three complete indicators with no mention of the other two, to avoid drawing attention to the gap.

debrief.correct: Submitting verified data for the three available indicators, explaining the gap honestly, and providing a corrective action plan demonstrates good faith and administrative transparency. NHIA reviewers are trained to distinguish between facilities that acknowledge and address gaps and those that conceal them. A credible plan with a realistic timeline is treated as evidence of a functioning quality system, not as grounds for immediate penalty.
debrief.wrong: Submitting estimated or nationally averaged values in place of facility-specific data is data fabrication. If discovered, this can result in immediate revocation of accreditation eligibility. Requesting an extension without submitting anything leaves the hospital formally non-compliant for the entire extension period, which creates its own risk. Submitting an incomplete report with no explanation is treated as a non-compliant submission — NHIA reviewers will identify the missing required indicators and flag the omission as more serious than a disclosed gap would have been.
debrief.rule_cited: NHIA accreditation standards require quarterly submission of all five designated core indicators; undisclosed gaps in required data are treated as non-compliance.
